functional.text: When a user clicks an ad, record the click and redirect them to the advertiser's landing page.
Aggregate clicks per ad per minute (and per hour/day).
Advertisers query click counts for their ads and campaigns over time ranges up to 90 days.
Duplicate clicks (double clicks, retries, replayed links) are counted once.

non_functional.text: Redirect latency < 50 ms at p99; the redirect must not depend on aggregation being up.
No click is lost, and billing counts are exact (reconciled daily).

assumptions.text: 1B clicks/day, peaks of ~5× average during big events; ~10M active ads.
~200 bytes per click event; raw clicks kept 90 days for audit.

out_of_scope.text: Ad serving and auctions, click-fraud models (beyond dedup), billing itself.

api.notes: The ad link points here; the signature lets us trust ad_id and dedupe by impression.

api.request: ad_id or campaign_id, time range, granularity
api.notes: Served from rollups; picks the coarsest table that answers the request.

data.name: click_events
data.fields: impression_id (dedup key), ad_id, campaign_id, event_time, user_agent, ip_hash
data.why: Append-only, partitioned by ad_id; archived as Parquet in object storage for 90 days.

data.name: ad_clicks_minute
data.fields: ad_id, campaign_id, minute, clicks (primary key ad_id + minute)
data.why: Pre-aggregated rollup in a columnar OLAP store; upserted by the stream job, overwritten by reconciliation.

parts.title: Click ingestion and redirect
parts.problem: Send the user to the advertiser's page within ~50 ms, at up to ~60k clicks/s, and never lose a click even if downstream processing is down.

options.name: insert each click into a database, then redirect
options.cons: 60k inserts/s on the redirect path; a slow DB delays every user

options.name: redirect immediately, send the click from the browser as a beacon
options.pros: zero server work on the path
options.cons: ad blockers and closed tabs lose clicks; easy to forge

options.name: click service appends the event to a durable log (acks from replicas), then 302
options.pros: ~5 ms append; the log buffers bursts and outages downstream
options.cons: another system to run; the event must be self-describing

parts.choice: stateless click service behind a load balancer appends the click to Kafka (partitioned by ad_id, acks=all) and answers 302 to the landing URL
parts.why: An append is a few ms and survives a broker loss, so N1 and N2 both hold; aggregation can lag or restart without touching the user's redirect. Partitioning by ad_id keeps one ad's clicks together for windowing.

parts.title: Stream aggregation per ad per minute
parts.problem: Turn ~12k clicks/s (peak ~60k) into counts per ad per minute that are visible within a minute, even when events arrive late or out of order.

options.name: increment a counter row per click
options.cons: a write per click; viral ads become hot rows

options.name: hourly batch job over raw clicks
options.cons: dashboards up to an hour stale (breaks N3)

options.name: stream processor with 1-minute tumbling windows keyed by ad_id, on event time with watermarks
options.pros: one write per ad per minute; late events handled explicitly; state is checkpointed
options.cons: operating a stateful stream job

parts.choice: Flink job: keyed by ad_id, 1-minute tumbling event-time windows, watermark = max event time − 30 s, late events up to 10 min update the window again
parts.why: Pre-aggregating in the stream turns ~700k clicks/min into at most one row per active ad per minute, and event time keeps a click in the minute it happened, not the minute it arrived.

nodes.label: Flink: 1-min windows per ad (event time, dedup)
OLAP store: clicks per ad per minute + hourly rollups

parts.title: Dedup and exactly-once counting
parts.problem: Count each real click exactly once although users double-click, bots replay links, the click service retries, and the stream job restarts from checkpoints.

options.name: count every event
options.cons: double clicks and retries inflate what advertisers pay

options.name: unique index on click_id in a database
options.cons: a DB write per click: the bottleneck we just removed

options.name: signed impression id per ad render; dedup in the stream job's keyed state with a TTL; idempotent upserts keyed (ad_id, minute)
options.pros: dedup in memory at stream speed; replays after a restart overwrite rather than add
options.cons: state size grows with the dedup window; checkpoints required

parts.choice: the ad server signs an impression_id into each ad link; Flink keeps seen impression_ids for 1 hour in checkpointed keyed state and drops repeats; window results are upserted (overwrite, not increment) by (ad_id, minute)
parts.why: A signature stops forged ids, the TTL bounds state (≈ 12k/s × 3,600 s × ~50 B ≈ 2 GB), and overwriting by key makes the sink idempotent, so replays after a crash cannot double-count.

nodes.label: Flink: 1-min windows per ad (event time, dedup)
OLAP store: clicks per ad per minute + hourly rollups

parts.title: Storage for advertiser queries
parts.problem: Answer 'clicks for my ads per minute/hour/day over the last 90 days', grouped by ad or campaign, in under a second.

options.name: query raw clicks in a row store
options.cons: scans billions of rows per dashboard load

options.name: key-value table keyed (ad_id, minute)
options.pros: fast for one ad's time range
options.cons: group-by across a campaign's ads means many reads and client-side sums

options.name: columnar OLAP store holding minute rollups, plus hourly and daily rollups
options.pros: fast scans and group-bys over pre-aggregated rows; time-partitioned retention
options.cons: another database; best with append/upsert batches, not single-row updates

parts.choice: columnar OLAP store (ClickHouse / Pinot / Druid class) partitioned by day: minute rollups for 7 days, hourly and daily rollups for 90 days; a query service picks the coarsest table that answers the request
parts.why: Pre-aggregated rows are ~100× fewer than raw clicks, so a 90-day campaign chart scans thousands of rows, not billions, and stays well under N4's 1 s.

nodes.label: OLAP store: clicks per ad per minute + hourly rollups

parts.title: Reconciliation with batch
parts.problem: Billing must be exact even if the stream job had a bug, dropped very late events, or was replayed: provide a source of truth and a way to correct the counts.

options.name: trust the stream counts
options.cons: a stream bug silently misbills until someone notices

options.name: replay Kafka through a fixed job (kappa)
options.cons: Kafka retention must cover the window; replays compete with live traffic

options.name: archive raw clicks to object storage; nightly batch recomputes exact daily counts and overwrites the rollups (lambda)
options.pros: independent check; exact numbers for billing; easy backfills
options.cons: two code paths to keep in agreement

parts.choice: Kafka sink writes raw clicks to object storage hourly; a nightly Spark job recomputes per-ad daily counts with the same dedup rules, overwrites them in the OLAP store, and alerts when stream and batch differ by more than 0.1%
parts.why: Advertisers are billed per click, so the daily number must come from a full, replayable source; the stream stays the fast path, and the batch is both the correction and the alarm.

nodes.label: OLAP store: clicks per ad per minute + hourly rollups

deep_dives.title: Late and out-of-order events

options.name: processing-time windows
options.cons: a click delayed 2 minutes is counted in the wrong minute

options.name: event-time windows with a watermark, drop anything later
options.cons: drops late clicks: billing undercounts

options.name: event-time windows, watermark − 30 s, allowed lateness 10 min, later still → side output fixed by the nightly batch
options.pros: correct and fresh; nothing is silently lost
options.cons: windows re-fire updates; needs an idempotent sink

deep_dives.choice: event-time windows, 30 s watermark delay, 10 min allowed lateness, later events to a side output that the nightly batch covers
deep_dives.why: N3 wants results within a minute, N2 wants none lost: the watermark bounds the wait, re-fired windows upsert the same key, and the batch is the backstop for stragglers.

deep_dives.title: A viral ad (hot partition)

options.name: partition by ad_id only
options.pros: all of an ad's clicks in one task
options.cons: one ad at 20k clicks/s overloads one partition and one task

options.name: salt hot ad_ids into N sub-keys, pre-aggregate per sub-key, then merge
options.cons: a second aggregation step

deep_dives.choice: salt detected hot ad_ids into N sub-keys and merge per minute
deep_dives.why: Counts are additive, so partial sums per sub-key merge exactly; only the few hot ads pay the extra step.

wrapup.bottlenecks: Hot ads on one Kafka partition / Flink task (salt them), the dedup state size (TTL), and OLAP ingest (batch upserts per minute rather than per click).
wrapup.failures: Flink crash: restart from the last checkpoint and replay Kafka; idempotent upserts mean no double counts. OLAP down: Flink buffers / Kafka retains, dashboards go stale, redirects unaffected. Click service: stateless behind the LB; if Kafka is unreachable, buffer briefly on local disk and still redirect.
wrapup.monitoring: Redirect p99, Kafka consumer lag, watermark delay, late-event count, dedup drop rate, stream vs batch difference per day, OLAP query p99.
wrapup.scale: 10× clicks: more Kafka partitions and Flink parallelism (both keyed by ad_id), more OLAP shards by time; the redirect tier scales horizontally.
wrapup.future: Impressions and conversions in the same pipeline, click-fraud scoring, per-advertiser real-time budget alerts.
